cells.tense: The drive is running and nothing in you has closed against what might come back.
cells.ask: Before you commit to the next step, say the number out loud and name one thing you'd change if it came back different. You keep the plan and the ear, and you'll know which one was driving.
cells.core:
The aim is steady, and the listening is steady with it. On an ordinary day you set the next thing in motion and leave room for the answer to land differently than you guessed — an email goes out, a reply comes back saying something you didn't plan for, and you read it before you decide what it changes. Nothing is being held back and nothing is being forced, so you can hear what's coming while you're still moving toward it, and the goal stays yours because you're still the one steering it.

Keep both hands in it — the aim and the ear. What it gives back is a next step that's yours, not just urgent.
cells.sheetLine: You aim and you listen, and neither is costing you the other.
cells.verb: to stay open to what's arriving before you've aimed at it
cells.place: the part of you that keeps a goal in motion

cells.tense: You're already living past the moment you're standing in, bracing for a future that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick the goal you're pushing hardest and write down what finishing it will actually give you, in one line. Then ask whether that line is true of the goal or true of the pressure. What comes back tells you which one you're serving.
cells.core:
On a good day the aim is steady and you're still in the room while you chase it — you notice the answer arriving and let it change the plan, and the timing feels like yours. What's happening instead is that the push has run ahead into a finish line you can't see yet, and you're living there instead of here, so every reply, every delay, gets read as a verdict on the future rather than as information about now. That rush is crowding out the very thing that would tell you if you're on course, which is what's actually in front of you. The momentum is real, and it's carrying you past the moment it exists to serve.

What it gives back is room to pick the aim you actually want instead of the one the pressure picked.

cells.tense: Part of you is still at a door that closed behind you, and the direction has gone quiet with it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you'd do today if the plan wasn't allowed to matter — one small act with no outcome attached. Do it before the day ends and see what it's like to want something with nothing riding on it.
cells.core:
When this is working you move toward what you want and the next fresh thing can still reach you. You come across a suggestion, a person, a way of doing something you hadn't tried, and you try it that week — not because it's strategic, just because it caught you. What's happening instead is that the line has gone slack, and no amount of pushing brings it back, because there's nothing in it to push. The aim isn't broken. The muscle for aiming needs charging, and it comes back from the smallest fresh act, not the biggest effort.

What it gives back is a thread of direction that doesn't need the whole plan behind it yet.

cells.tense: You're already steering by something you haven't named, in a present you keep calling automatic.
cells.ask: Pick one decision you've been calling obvious and say whose it is — one sentence, addressed to no one in particular. You'll know immediately whether it was yours. That's the whole experiment.
cells.core:
When this is working you know what you want directly and act on it without argument — a call gets made, the next thing starts, and you're comfortable not having it all figured out in advance. What's happening instead is that the steering is going on — you're making calls, keeping momentum — as if the direction came with the day rather than from you. The direction is real. The claiming of it isn't, and that's what keeps you from being able to change it when you want to. Saying it aloud costs nothing and hands the call back to the one who's already making it.

What it gives back is knowing which of your next moves is a decision and which is just a habit wearing one.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I had to cut every time: 'you're afraid of what you'll feel' — the record says the vessel is open or closed, not that fear is in it, and the person never told me. A reader could say 'that's not avoidance, that's just how I plan' and still use the experiment, because the experiment is one sentence out loud, not a demand to feel something. The sentence that serves me rather than the reader would be any line where the open heart sounds like a prize; the cell has to offer the plain act and let them decide what it's worth.
